If you’re pondering beauty, producing efficiently, and working across aisles – same. Here are some sticky thoughts on the other side of config 2025.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 2](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*ht0MLlsIZJJpyYASbWi-dw.png)

**Less Handoffs, way more Hands-On:**  
Figma’s made four big extensions to their tool: Figma Make, Figma Sites, Figma Buzz, and Illustrator, but it’s called Figma Draw. Full circle. I’ve spent the last 3 years building janky workflows for what Figma Buzz now does natively in the app. God bless. For us as designers, that means we just continue to get a heck of a lot more powerful and what we’re able to deliver on. Challenge by choice there I think.

We need to sharpen both our concepts and our execution. It’s not enough to have the vision — can you produce it on your own, prototype it, pitch it, and then publish it too? The answer is yes.

**On-brand and at scale:**  
Your design system is only as strong as the worst asset that goes out the door. Buzz’s logic based, AI-assisted (?) production workflow is geared at empowering marketing teams to produce huge volume without creative bottlenecks. I think this workflow is going to only be as successful as the marketing orgs willingness to get on board with it. Meaning, the content structure, the designs themselves, and the use case might have to be just right for this one to be as impactful as it can be.

Think of these new Figma products not as new tools to learn, but as new mindsets to work in. You know the tool. It’s Figma. Now poke around and think a bit more like a product designer.

**Robinhood Rebrand:**  
Felipe Rocha and Carlo Michelangelo Luetto’s talk on the Robinhood rebrand was a fabulous end to the conference. One of the only (if not _the_ only brand ID-focused convo of the whole event.) The work was nice. Not because it was loud, or over the top — but because it was a centered presentation of the core elements of brand. Unbothered by industry noise, it was just beautiful work which was thoughtfully considered for the business. It showed that the best brands today are the ones that leave room for evolution when they are applied. Huge shout out to this client-agency partnership as work was shared before and after delivery. I don’t know if they are going to release the video, but trust it was damn faithful application of the brand in an ad spot.

What this means for us: context is everything. Complexity is a pain. An incredible reminder that in the era of AI everything, great work continues to be simple, confident, and laser-focused on the goal.

**Linear and the Return to Craft:**  
To that end, Karri from Linear made a simple but resonant point: craft matters. In a time where 80% of the work can be generated at lightspeed, your slow taste, care, and discernment are what set the work apart.

**My big idea from the week:**  
As these super powerful ways of working are made possible, the sexy, cool, underground thing is gonna be the slow, painstaking work. Notice how fine artists will double down in handmade intricacy. If you design for a large brand, look for ways to insert the indescribable, classic, analog arts into your work. The hand-painted, eyeballed work will get hot. The obvious time-spent on a work will carry way more meaning.

I’m getting on the Renaissance bandwagon. Not the Cowboy Carter one, but the school of thought, Renaissance 2.0 one. The move away from tech and logic and KPIs and OKRs and performance and the move toward art for arts sake. Art and design for the sake of human dignity. More to come on this, I’m pretty interested in this movement.

**Too long, didn’t read a damn thing?**  
Everything’s exactly the same, just a little different this time around. Easy as that. It’s Illustrator again, it’s production design with a friendlier face, it’s code, its optics. Industries are noisy and full of ulterior motives— you want quiet? pick up painting. Seriously. I want to remind designers out there that the fundamentals stay the same. Focus on your craft. Do the damned reading, fill your sketchbook, and put in the work. Advocate for opportunities that grow yourself and your team and get an understanding of what’s happening under the hood. A good litmus test as you generate work: are you proud to sign your name on it? If not, put way more of your heart into it.
